app.name: Hololemma
landing.tagline: A holographic lab you control with your bare hands.
landing.subtitle: Take a human heart and a robot dog apart in mid-air, study every piece, then put them back together. All you need is a laptop webcam.

heart.title: Human heart
heart.summary: Four chambers, four valves and the vessels that carry blood in and out — from a real human scan.
heart.credit: Heart and vessels: Human Reference Atlas (HuBMAP), Visible Human Male, CC BY 4.0.
heart.info.right_atrium.desc: The right atrium collects oxygen-poor blood coming back from the body through the two venae cavae, and from the heart muscle itself through the coronary sinus. When it contracts, it pushes this blood through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
heart.info.right_atrium.fact: Its wall holds the sinoatrial (SA) node — the heart's natural pacemaker that starts every heartbeat.
heart.info.left_atrium.desc: The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs through the four pulmonary veins and passes it through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.
heart.info.left_atrium.fact: It is the chamber closest to your back — it sits right in front of the oesophagus, the tube that carries food to your stomach.
heart.info.right_ventricle.desc: The right ventricle pumps oxygen-poor blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and on to the lungs. The lungs are close by, so its wall is thinner than the left ventricle’s.
heart.info.right_ventricle.fact: Seen from the front, most of the heart's front surface is actually the right ventricle.
heart.info.left_ventricle.desc: The left ventricle is the heart's main pump. It pushes oxygen-rich blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and out to the whole body. It also forms the heart's tip, the apex.
heart.info.left_ventricle.fact: Its wall is about three times thicker than the right ventricle’s, because it has to push blood all the way to your toes.
heart.info.septum.desc: The septum is the muscular wall between the left and right ventricles. It keeps oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood apart and helps both ventricles squeeze.
heart.info.septum.fact: Special conducting fibres run along it, spreading the electrical signal that makes both ventricles contract together.
heart.info.tricuspid_valve.desc: The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and the right ventricle. Its three flaps open to let blood into the ventricle, then shut so blood cannot flow back when the ventricle contracts.
heart.info.tricuspid_valve.fact: Closing valves make the sounds of your heartbeat: the first sound, the 'lub', is the tricuspid and mitral valves shutting.
heart.info.mitral_valve.desc: The mitral valve lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle. It has only two flaps, so it is also called the bicuspid valve.
heart.info.mitral_valve.fact: It is named after a bishop's mitre (hat), because its two flaps look like one.
heart.info.pulmonary_valve.desc: The pulmonary valve guards the exit of the right ventricle. It opens when the ventricle pushes blood into the pulmonary trunk, then closes so the blood cannot fall back.
heart.info.pulmonary_valve.fact: When it closes together with the aortic valve, it makes the second heart sound — the 'dub'.
heart.info.aortic_valve.desc: The aortic valve sits at the exit of the left ventricle. It opens to let blood rush into the aorta and closes between beats so blood doesn't leak back.
heart.info.aortic_valve.fact: The openings of the heart's own coronary arteries sit just above its flaps.
heart.info.papillary_muscles.desc: Papillary muscles are small pillars of muscle inside the ventricles. Thin cords called chordae tendineae tie them to the flaps of the tricuspid and mitral valves (the cords are too fine to appear in this model).
heart.info.papillary_muscles.fact: They tighten as the ventricles squeeze, so the valve flaps can’t flip backwards — like ropes holding a sail.
heart.info.aorta.desc: The aorta is the body's largest artery. It carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle, curves over the heart in the aortic arch, then runs down through the chest and belly. Branches from the arch supply the head and arms.
heart.info.aorta.fact: In adults it is about as wide as a garden hose — roughly 2.5 to 3 cm across.
heart.info.pulmonary_trunk.desc: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle and splits into the left and right pulmonary arteries, which carry oxygen-poor blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen.
heart.info.pulmonary_trunk.fact: The pulmonary arteries are the only arteries in an adult that carry oxygen-poor blood.
heart.info.pulmonary_veins.desc: Four pulmonary veins — two from each lung — bring freshly oxygenated blood back to the left atrium.
heart.info.pulmonary_veins.fact: They are the only veins in an adult that carry oxygen-rich blood.
heart.info.superior_vena_cava.desc: The superior vena cava is a large vein that brings oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck, arms and upper chest into the right atrium.
heart.info.superior_vena_cava.fact: Unlike many veins in your arms and legs, it has no valve where it opens into the heart.
heart.info.inferior_vena_cava.desc: The inferior vena cava is the body's largest vein. It carries oxygen-poor blood from the legs, belly and lower body up into the right atrium.
heart.info.inferior_vena_cava.fact: It runs up beside the aorta, on the right side of the spine.
heart.info.left_coronary_artery.desc: The left coronary artery starts just above the aortic valve and feeds the heart muscle itself — mainly the left ventricle and the septum. It soon divides into branches that run over the heart’s surface.
heart.info.left_coronary_artery.fact: Even though the heart is full of blood, its muscle can't take oxygen from the blood inside it — it relies on these arteries.
heart.info.right_coronary_artery.desc: The right coronary artery also begins just above the aortic valve. It runs in the groove between the right atrium and the right ventricle and supplies the right side of the heart.
heart.info.right_coronary_artery.fact: In most people it also supplies the SA node, the heart's pacemaker.
heart.info.cardiac_veins.desc: The cardiac veins collect oxygen-poor blood from the heart muscle. Most drain into the coronary sinus, a wide vein on the back of the heart that empties into the right atrium.
heart.info.cardiac_veins.fact: The great cardiac vein runs right beside the left coronary artery, like a return lane next to a road.
heart.hint.septum: The septum is the base of the heart model.
heart.hint.ventricle: The ventricles are built around the septum — place the septum first.
heart.hint.right_atrium: The right atrium sits above the right ventricle — place the right ventricle first.
heart.hint.left_atrium: The left atrium sits above the left ventricle — place the left ventricle first.
heart.hint.papillary_muscles: Papillary muscles grow from the inner walls of the ventricles — place both ventricles first.
heart.hint.tricuspid_valve: The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle, and its cords tie to the papillary muscles — place those first.
heart.hint.mitral_valve: The mitral valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle, and its cords tie to the papillary muscles — place those first.
heart.hint.pulmonary_valve: This valve guards the exit of the right ventricle — place the right ventricle first.
heart.hint.aortic_valve: This valve guards the exit of the left ventricle — place the left ventricle first.
heart.hint.pulmonary_trunk: The pulmonary trunk starts at the pulmonary valve — place the valve first.
heart.hint.aorta: The aorta starts at the aortic valve — place the valve first.
heart.hint.pulmonary_veins: These veins empty into the left atrium — place the left atrium first.
heart.hint.vena_cava: The venae cavae empty into the right atrium — place the right atrium first.
heart.hint.coronary_artery: The coronary arteries branch off the aorta just above the aortic valve — place the aorta first.
heart.hint.cardiac_veins: The cardiac veins run beside the coronary arteries and drain into the right atrium — place the coronary arteries and the right atrium first.
robotDog.title: Robot dog
robotDog.summary: A real open-source quadruped: 12 motors, a computer, a battery and a laser scanner on four legs.
robotDog.credit: Robot dog based on Mini Pupper 2 by MangDang, Apache License 2.0. Servos and battery modelled by Hololemma.
robotDog.info.frame.desc: The frame is the robot's skeleton. Every other part is fixed to it, so it has to be light but stiff — the legs need something solid to push against.
robotDog.info.frame.fact: Engineers use the frame as the robot's reference point (the 'base link') when they describe where every other part is.
robotDog.info.battery.desc: The rechargeable lithium battery stores energy for the motors, the computer and the sensors. It sits low and near the middle so the weight stays balanced.
robotDog.info.battery.fact: When the robot jumps or climbs, all twelve motors pull current at once — the battery must deliver strong bursts of power, not just store energy.
robotDog.info.controller_board.desc: The main circuit board carries a small computer, power circuits and connectors. It runs the control loop: read the sensors, decide, and send new angles to every motor many times per second.
robotDog.info.controller_board.fact: It also holds an IMU (inertial measurement unit) — a tiny chip that senses tilt and acceleration, so the robot knows when it is about to fall.
robotDog.info.servos.desc: Each leg has three servo motors: one swings the leg out to the side, one swings the upper leg forward and back at the hip, and one bends the knee. A servo is a motor with gears and a sensor that can hold any angle it is told.
robotDog.info.servos.fact: Twelve servos give the robot 12 'degrees of freedom' — 3 per leg, the minimum for a foot to reach any point beneath it.
robotDog.info.hip.desc: The hip module joins the leg to the body and holds the leg's motors. It tilts the whole leg in or out to keep the robot balanced.
robotDog.info.hip.fact: Putting the heavy motors at the hip, close to the body, keeps the legs light and quick to swing.
robotDog.info.upper_leg.desc: The upper leg (thigh) swings forward and back from the hip, like your own thigh when you walk.
robotDog.info.upper_leg.fact: Robot legs are made light on purpose: the less weight at the end of a leg, the less force a motor needs to swing it.
robotDog.info.lower_leg.desc: The lower leg bends at the knee and ends in a rubber foot that grips the floor. Upper and lower leg work together like your thigh and shin.
robotDog.info.lower_leg.fact: The foot is the only part that touches the ground — the grip there is what lets the robot push itself forward.
robotDog.info.lidar.desc: LiDAR spins a laser beam and measures how long the light takes to bounce back. That builds a 360° map of distances, so the robot can avoid walls and map a room.
robotDog.info.lidar.fact: Light travels about 30 cm in one billionth of a second — LiDAR measures time that precisely.
robotDog.info.front_plate.desc: The front plate closes the body at the front and protects the electronics behind it.
robotDog.info.front_plate.fact: Covers go on last in real robot building too, so engineers can test the wiring before closing everything up.
robotDog.info.side_shells.desc: The side shells cover the body and keep dust and fingers away from the moving parts and circuits inside.
robotDog.info.side_shells.fact: A shell also stiffens the body, a bit like how an egg shell is strong for its weight.
robotDog.hint.frame: The frame is the base of the robot.
robotDog.hint.battery: The battery sits inside the frame — place the frame first.
robotDog.hint.controller_board: The board needs power — place the battery first so it can be wired in.
robotDog.hint.servos: Motors need power and commands — place the controller board first.
robotDog.hint.hip: The hip module mounts on this leg's servos — place them first.
robotDog.hint.upper_leg: The upper leg attaches to the hip module — place the hip first.
robotDog.hint.lower_leg: The lower leg hangs from the knee at the end of the upper leg — place the upper leg first.
robotDog.hint.lidar: The LiDAR plugs into the controller board — place the board first.
robotDog.hint.front_plate: Covers go on last so you can still reach the wiring — place the board and the LiDAR first.
robotDog.hint.side_shells: The shells close the body — finish the inside first: battery, board and all four sets of servos.
panel.explodeHint: Pinch with both hands near the model and pull apart.
panel.cutawayHint: Slice the model open to see inside.
study.howToOpen: Tip: hold a part with one hand, then pinch with the other and pull away to study it.
assembly.title: Assembly
assembly.instructions: Pinch a part on the bench and carry it to its glowing outline.
assembly.completeHint: Every part is back in place.
credits.title: Credits
credits.fonts: Fonts: Inter and JetBrains Mono (SIL Open Font License).
credits.tracking: Hand tracking: MediaPipe by Google (Apache License 2.0), running entirely in your browser.
landing.step1Text: Hololemma watches your hands through the webcam. The video never leaves your computer.
landing.step2Text: Hold up both open palms for three seconds so the lab can learn the size of your hands.
landing.step3Text: Pinch to grab and turn. Pinch with both hands and pull apart to take a model to pieces — then rebuild it.
landing.librarySubtitle: Choose a model. More are on the way.
landing.privacyText: Hand tracking runs entirely inside your browser. No video or images are uploaded, stored or recorded — ever.
landing.needsLaptop: Open on a laptop with a webcam
landing.needsLaptopText: Hololemma uses your hands in front of a webcam, so it needs a laptop or desktop computer with Chrome or Edge.
landing.mouseNote: No webcam? You can still explore with a mouse.
tips.title: Gestures
tips.pinchText: Turns the model. Let go and it keeps spinning a little.
tips.pull: Pinch with both hands near the model, pull apart
tips.pullText: Takes it to pieces. Push your hands together to close it.
tips.grabText: Pick it up. Pinch with your other hand and pull away to study it.
tips.dwellText: Hold still until it fills — or pinch it.
tips.fist: Make a fist for a second
tips.mouse: Mouse: drag to turn, scroll to zoom, double-click a part to study it.
